Maitreyi.description: The daughter of engineer Narendra Sen, Maitreyi is the central female figure of the novel, whose mysterious beauty and presence captivate the narrator.

Narendra Sen.description: A respected Bengali engineer, Maitreyi's father, and the narrator's employer and patron in Calcutta.

Harold Carr.description: Harold Carr is the narrator's roommate at Ripon Mansion and an employee at the Army and Navy Stores; he is part of Allan's expatriate social group in Calcutta.

Lucien Metz.description: A French journalist and acquaintance of the narrator, visiting India to write a book and eager to learn about Indian society.

Bhowanipore.description: A district in Calcutta (now Kolkata), known for its residential neighborhoods and Bengali culture.

Oxford Book Stationary.description: A book and stationery shop in Calcutta, a colonial-era establishment frequented by the educated class.

Ripon Mansion.description: A residential building on Wellesley Street in Calcutta where the narrator lives.

Army and Navy Stores.description: A British colonial department store in Calcutta catering to Europeans and the colonial elite.

Y.M.C.A..description: Young Men's Christian Association, a social and recreational club popular among Europeans in colonial India.

Rotary Club.description: An international service organization with local chapters, including one in Calcutta, often frequented by professionals and elites.

Noel and Noel.description: A company or factory referenced as the narrator's former employer, likely a British or European business in colonial India.

Clive Street.description: A major commercial street in Calcutta, known for its colonial-era offices and businesses.

Tamluk.description: A town in West Bengal, India, where the narrator oversees construction work.

Howrah-Madras express.description: A long-distance train connecting Howrah (Calcutta's main station) with Madras (now Chennai), indicative of colonial rail travel.

Howrah.description: The main railway station in Calcutta and a city across the Hooghly River, serving as a transportation hub.

Capstan.description: A popular British brand of pipe tobacco, favored by the narrator.

Bengal.description: A region in eastern India, known for its distinct culture, language, and landscape.

Hindusthani.description: A colloquial term for the Hindustani language, a lingua franca in northern India combining elements of Hindi and Urdu.

Aden.description: A port city in Yemen, historically a stopover for ships traveling between Europe and India.

Malaya.description: A historical region in Southeast Asia, now part of Malaysia, referenced as part of Lucien's travels.

Mahatma Gandhi.description: The prominent Indian leader of the independence movement, referenced for his influence and reputation.

Paris.description: The capital of France, mentioned as the publication city for Lucien's planned book.

Brahmin.description: The highest caste in the traditional Hindu social hierarchy, associated with priests and scholars.

Calcutta Club.description: An exclusive social club in Calcutta, frequented by the city's elite.

Kashmiri.description: Relating to Kashmir, a region in northern India known for its fine wool and handicrafts.

sahib.description: A term of respect used in colonial India to address or refer to European men.

Eurasian.description: A person of mixed European and Asian (usually Indian) descent, often occupying a distinct social position in colonial society.

purdah.description: A social and religious practice of female seclusion prevalent among some Muslim and Hindu communities in India.

sari.description: A traditional Indian garment for women, consisting of a long piece of cloth draped around the body.

shawl.description: A piece of fabric worn over the shoulders or head, commonly used in Indian attire.

calico.description: A type of plain-woven cotton fabric, often printed with simple patterns, commonly used for dresses in India.

Lucien.description: A friend or acquaintance of the narrator, shown Sanskrit manuscripts by the engineer.

Norinne.description: A woman from the narrator's social circle, recently engaged, with whom the narrator once had romantic feelings.

Eddy Higgering.description: A man from the narrator's past, involved in a conflict and boxing match with the narrator.

Geurtie.description: A woman in the narrator's social circle, who accompanies him to a banquet and sits on his knees.

Allan.description: Allan is the narrator and protagonist, a European engineer working in India; he is based on Mircea Eliade, the Romanian intellectual whose experiences and feelings form the core of the novel.

Sanskrit.description: An ancient classical language of India, in which many religious and philosophical texts are written.

Calcutta.description: A major city in eastern India, known today as Kolkata, and the primary setting of the novel.

Lakes.description: Refers to a recreational area, likely the lakes in or near Calcutta, popular for outings.

Assam.description: A state in northeastern India, known for its tea plantations and jungles.

Lumding-Sadyia.description: A railway line in Assam, India, referenced as the site of engineering work.

Society.description: Refers to the professional or engineering society employing the narrator, which is swarajist.

Park Street.description: A famous street in Calcutta, known for its nightlife and restaurants.

Chowringhee Road.description: A major thoroughfare in Calcutta, central to the city's colonial and commercial life.

Dhurmtollah Street.description: A well-known street in Calcutta, intersecting with other major roads.

Ganges.description: A sacred river in India, central to Hindu religious practices.

Council.description: The governing or administrative body of the Society or company employing the narrator.

Sikh.description: A member of a religious community originating in the Punjab region, known for their distinct identity and often serving in the military or as drivers.

pandit.description: A learned scholar or teacher, especially in Sanskrit and Hindu law, philosophy, or religion.

telegram.description: A message sent by telegraph, a common means of urgent communication in the early 20th century.

pajama party.description: A social gathering where guests wear pajamas, reflecting Westernized customs among expatriates.

banquet.description: A formal meal or feast, often for celebration.

bahut achhal.description: Hindi phrase meaning 'very good' or 'very nice.'

Clara.description: A friend of Allan, who visits him in the hospital with Geurtie.

Mr. Frank.description: A Eurasian who helps identify Allan's illness as malaria and arranges for his care.

Mr. Carr.description: A person at the hospital whom the nurse refers to, likely a staff member or doctor.

Catherine.description: A friend of Allan, mentioned as concerned for his health.

Huber.description: Refers to the Huber brothers, acquaintances of Allan, one of whom is associated with Ivy.

Ivy.description: A beautiful woman associated with the Huber brothers.

Simpsons.description: Refers to two individuals, Isaac and Gerald, known for their questionable behavior at social gatherings.

Isaac.description: One of the Simpsons, known for hiding and drinking whisky neat.

Gerald.description: One of the Simpsons, known for stealing cigarettes at parties.

Mrs. Sen.description: Mrs. Sen, also known as Srimati Devi Indira, is Narendra Sen's wife and Maitreyi's mother, depicted as youthful and timid, with limited English proficiency.

Anglo-Indians.description: A community of mixed Indian and British ancestry, prominent in colonial India, often forming their own social circles.

Shillong.description: A hill station in northeast India, known for its cool climate and as a retreat from the plains.

Sadyia.description: A town in Assam, located in a remote area near the Brahmaputra River.

European hospital.description: A hospital in colonial India designated for Europeans, reflecting the racial segregation of the era.

Wellesley Street.description: A street in Calcutta, indicative of the colonial urban landscape.

Middle Bank.description: Likely refers to a bank or financial institution in Calcutta.

Firpos.description: A famous European-style restaurant and nightclub in colonial Calcutta.

Out of the East.description: A book by Lafcadio Hearn, reflecting cross-cultural literary interests.

Lord Jim.description: A novel by Joseph Conrad, referenced in the context of literary discussion.

Almayer’s Folly.description: Another novel by Joseph Conrad, mentioned as Allan's favorite.

bungalow.description: A single-story house with a veranda, typical of colonial architecture in India.

veranda.description: A roofed, open-air porch attached to a house, common in Indian homes.

soda siphon.description: A pressurized bottle used to dispense carbonated water, popular in colonial drinks.

pajamas.description: Loose-fitting clothes for sleeping or lounging, originally from South Asia.

monsoon.description: The seasonal heavy rains characteristic of the Indian subcontinent.

annas.description: A former unit of currency in India, equal to 1/16 of a rupee.

Mr. Sen.description: Mr. Sen (also referred to as Sen, baba, or babà) is the Indian engineer and head of the household where Allan is staying; he is Maitreyi's father and Allan's superior, whose approval is crucial for Maitreyi's engagement.

David.description: The elder Huber brother, mentioned as someone with a car who might be invited to a gathering.

Bengali.description: The language spoken by the Sen family and many in Calcutta; also refers to the culture of Bengal.

maidan.description: A large open parkland or field, commonly found in Indian cities; in Calcutta, the Maidan is a famous central park.

Count Lew Tolstoy.description: Refers to Leo Tolstoy, the famous Russian writer known for his philosophical and literary works.

Italian legation.description: The diplomatic mission or embassy of Italy in Calcutta, a place of social gatherings for expatriates.

University.description: Refers to the University of Calcutta, a prestigious institution where Maitreyi is preparing for her Bachelor of Arts.

Bachelor of Arts.description: An undergraduate academic degree awarded for a course or program in the arts or sciences.

Tagore.description: Rabindranath Tagore, also known as Robi Thakkur in Bengali, is a renowned Bengali poet, philosopher, and Nobel laureate, admired by Maitreyi and her family.

matriculation.description: The process of qualifying for entry to a university, often through a standardized exam.

French.description: Refers to the French language, which the narrator teaches to Maitreyi as part of their cultural exchange.

dowry.description: A sum of money or property brought by a bride to her husband upon marriage, a traditional practice in Indian society.

custom.description: A traditional practice or usual way of doing something specific to a culture or community.

giacè.description: A Bengali expression meaning 'I’m coming now.'

ki vishan.description: A Bengali exclamation expressing wonder or surprise, similar to 'how extraordinary!'

caste.description: A hereditary social class in Hindu society, traditionally restricting the occupation of its members and their association with the members of other castes.

pantheist.description: A person who believes that God or divinity is identical with the universe or nature; here, used to describe Maitreyi's spiritual worldview.

idyll.description: A simple, peaceful, or romantic scene, often used to describe an idealized relationship or situation.

Mantu.description: The engineer's cousin, recently arrived from Delhi to become a lecturer and to get married; he becomes a friend to the narrator.

Khokha.description: A young man, a poor relative of the engineer, who stays in the house during Mantu's wedding and entertains with jokes.

Phul.description: A fictional character, the king's son in Chabù's story, symbolizing innocence and wonder.

Keora atar.description: A traditional Indian perfume distilled from the flowers of the pandanus plant, popular in Bengal.

Puri.description: A coastal city in the Indian state of Odisha, famous for its beaches and religious significance.

L’Inde avec les Anglais.description: A French book titled 'India with the English', written by Lucien, reflecting on colonial India.

Valéry.description: Refers to Paul Valéry, a renowned French poet, mentioned as a standard for romantic poetry.

Anactoria.description: A poem by Algernon Charles Swinburne, referenced during a literary discussion between the narrator and Maitreyi.

Government Commercial School.description: An educational institution in Delhi where Mantu previously taught.

Delhi.description: The capital city of India, where Mantu lived before coming to Calcutta.

atar.description: A natural perfume oil derived from botanical sources, commonly used in South Asia.

balustrade.description: A railing supported by balusters, commonly found on balconies or staircases.

guru.description: A spiritual teacher or guide in Indian culture, often revered by disciples.

nox.description: Latin for 'night', used here to refer to the first night of Mantu's wedding ceremony.

fiancée.description: A woman engaged to be married, used here in the context of the narrator's musings.

mouches volantes.description: French for 'flying flies', referring to floaters or spots in one's vision, often due to eye or blood pressure issues.

Lilu.description: A young woman, referred to as 'auntie' though only seventeen, who is part of the household's social circle and confides in Maitreyi about conjugal love.

Himansural Ray.description: An Indian film actor whose movie the characters watch at the cinema.

Shakuntala.description: A classic Sanskrit play by Kalidasa, widely regarded as a masterpiece of Indian literature.

Mahuya.description: A work by Tagore, from which Maitreyi recites poetry; it refers to one of his poetic or dramatic compositions.

Vallaka.description: Another work by Tagore, likely a collection of poems or a poetic drama.

England.description: Referenced as the place where a Bengali young man is studying, highlighting the colonial context.

France.description: Mentioned as the destination of the engineer's postponed journey, reflecting the cosmopolitan connections of the characters.

Rajputana.description: A historical region in northwestern India, known for its distinctive traditional costumes.

madam.description: A formal term of address for a woman, here contrasted with the Indian custom of calling a mother-in-law 'mother.'

auntie.description: A term of respect and affection for an older woman, not necessarily a blood relative, common in Indian culture.

nuptial bed.description: A phrase referring to the marriage bed, symbolizing consummation and marital union.

poetess.description: A female poet; used here to refer to Maitreyi.

platonic.description: Describing a relationship that is intimate and affectionate but not sexual.

meditation through contrary images.description: A mental exercise where one tries to suppress desire by imagining the object of affection in an unappealing way.

Iris.description: Iris is mentioned as someone for whom Harold goes to church, suggesting she is a significant person in Harold's life, possibly his wife or romantic interest.

Acintya.description: Acintya is a young Bengali poet, described as original and controversial, admired by Maitreyi and associated with the magazine Prabuddha Bharatta; he interacts with Maitreyi by telephone, sending poems for publication.

Ripon Street.description: Another street in Calcutta, similarly associated with the city's colonial-era social scene.

Prabuddha Bharatta.description: A prominent English-language monthly journal of the Ramakrishna Order, focused on spirituality and Indian culture.

Krishna.description: A major Hindu deity, central to the Vaishnav tradition, often associated with divine love and mysticism.

Vaishnavism.description: Vaishnavism is a major tradition within Hinduism devoted to the worship of Vishnu and his avatars; its followers are called Vaishnavas or Vaishnavs, emphasizing devotion and love.

Chaitanya.description: Refers to Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, a 16th-century Bengali saint and founder of the Gaudiya Vaishnavism movement, renowned for his ecstatic devotion to Krishna.

dhoti.description: A traditional men's garment in India, consisting of a long piece of cloth wrapped around the waist and legs.

mantra.description: A sacred utterance, word, or phrase in Sanskrit, believed to have spiritual power and used in meditation or prayer.

Shantiniketan.description: An educational and cultural institution founded by Rabindranath Tagore in West Bengal, known for its artistic and intellectual community.

India.description: The country in which the novel is set, specifically during the colonial period under British rule.

rajah.description: A term for an Indian king or prince, here used to evoke the fantasy of wealth and status in a foreign land.

English.description: Refers to the British colonial rulers of India, often contrasted with the Indian characters in terms of culture and power.

voluptuousness.description: A term describing sensual pleasure or delight, often used in the context of physical love.

betrothal.description: The formal engagement or promise to marry, here symbolized by the exchange of a jasmine garland.

Kalidasa.description: A celebrated classical Sanskrit poet and playwright, author of 'Shakuntala' and other works.

Alipore.description: A neighborhood in Calcutta (Kolkata), known for its affluent residences and colonial history.

Jaganath.description: Refers to Lord Jagannath, a form of the Hindu god Krishna, worshipped primarily at the Jagannath Temple in Puri.

Chandernagore.description: A former French colony and town near Calcutta, known for its colonial architecture and historical significance.

Barackpur.description: A town near Calcutta, historically significant as a British cantonment and site of early Indian uprisings.

Urwald.description: A German word meaning 'primeval forest,' used here to evoke the sense of an ancient, untouched jungle.

ashram.description: A spiritual hermitage or monastery in Indian religions, often a place for religious retreat and study.

Swami Vivekananda.description: A prominent Indian Hindu monk and spiritual leader, founder of the Ramakrishna Mission and influential in introducing Indian philosophies to the West.

Chattered Bank.description: Likely a reference to the Chartered Bank, a British colonial-era bank operating in India.

Gandhi.description: Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the Indian independence movement, known for his philosophy of nonviolent resistance.

Japan.description: Mentioned in the context of Japanese merchandise, reflecting the boycott of British goods during the nationalist movement.

Christianity.description: Christianity refers to the religion based on the teachings of Jesus Christ, contrasted in the novel with Hindu customs and morality.

Hinduism.description: The major religion of India, central to the beliefs and customs of Maitreyi's family.

Upanishads.description: Ancient Indian philosophical texts that form the theoretical basis for Hinduism, referenced for their spiritual teachings.

pcm.description: A Bengali term used here by Maitreyi to refer to a tree she loved as a child; possibly a child's word or nickname.

seven leaves.description: A colloquial or poetic reference to a type of tree with compound leaves, significant in Maitreyi's childhood story.

garland.description: A decorative wreath of flowers, often used in Indian rituals and as a symbol of betrothal or honor.

bodice.description: The fitted upper part of a woman's dress, here referring to the blouse worn under a sari.

karma.description: A concept in Indian religions referring to the sum of a person's actions and their consequences in this and future lives.

swadeshi.description: A nationalist movement and principle in India advocating the use of domestically produced goods and the boycott of foreign products.

Chabii.description: Chabii (also spelled Chabù) is the younger daughter of Narendra Sen, about ten or eleven years old, described as lively and resembling a gypsy girl; she is also referred to as Khokha’s sister and a widow, timid and overworked.

Indian marriage ceremony.description: Refers to the traditional Hindu wedding rituals, which involve symbolic jewelry and customs.

kirtan.description: A devotional singing or chanting of hymns, especially in the Vaishnava tradition.

scented with coconut oil.description: Refers to the common practice in India of applying coconut oil to hair or skin for fragrance and care.

betrothal bracelet.description: A traditional piece of jewelry given to a bride during engagement ceremonies in India, symbolizing commitment.

chaise longue.description: A chaise longue (also spelled chaise-longue) is a long reclining chair for relaxing, often used in colonial settings.

Allan-dadà.description: 'Dadà' is a Bengali term meaning 'elder brother,' used affectionately for an older male; 'Allan-dadà' is a term of endearment or respect used for Allan by the Sen family.

chauffeur.description: A driver, often for a private car; in colonial India, usually a servant employed by wealthy families.

beri-beri.description: A disease caused by vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency, leading to swelling and pain, mentioned as part of Maitreyi's health history.

Anasuya.description: A nickname used by Maitreyi and the narrator for a fictional friend, referenced in their discussions to disguise their true feelings.

Chatterji.description: A Bengali author, mentioned as the writer of 'Srikantha,' expected to attend Maitreyi's birthday celebration.

Uday Shankar.description: A famous Indian dancer known for his beauty and artistry, admired by Maitreyi and present at her birthday celebration.

Srikantha.description: A novel written by Chatterji, a notable work in Bengali literature.

James Joyce.description: An Irish modernist writer, referenced here for his novel 'Ulysses,' which influenced contemporary literature.

Ulysses.description: A groundbreaking modernist novel by James Joyce, known for its experimental style.

Midnapur.description: A town in West Bengal, India, mentioned as a place where the Sen family has relatives.

divan.description: A long, low sofa or couch, often without a back or arms, used for reclining.

Mrs. Ribeiro.description: The landlady of Allan's boarding house, a concerned and motherly figure.

Swami Madhvananda.description: A monk at Belur Math whom Allan visits for solace during his emotional crisis.

The Statesman.description: A prominent English-language newspaper published in Calcutta.

Darjeeling.description: A hill station in West Bengal, famous for its tea plantations and cool climate.

Gopalpur-at-Sea.description: A seaside town in Odisha, India, popular as a quiet retreat.

father Justus.description: A reference to a Catholic priest known to the characters, who recovered at Gopalpur-at-Sea.

Uddkita.description: A notebook or literary work in which Maitreyi writes her last words to Allan.

Hoogli.description: Hooghly (also spelled Hoogly or Hoogli) refers to a district and river near Calcutta, important in Bengal's history and culture.

Bengal Film Company.description: A film production company in Bengal, where Khokha is employed.

Kalighat.description: A neighborhood in Calcutta, famous for its Kali temple.

Royd Lane.description: A street in Calcutta, location of Allan's boarding house.

Howrah Bridge.description: A famous bridge spanning the Hooghly River, connecting Calcutta and Howrah.

Belur.description: Belur is a town near Calcutta, home to the headquarters of the Ramakrishna Mission; Belur-Math refers specifically to the monastery and headquarters of the Ramakrishna Mission located there.

Swami.description: A Hindu religious teacher or monk.

Ranaghat.description: A town in West Bengal, north of Calcutta.

Bally.description: A suburb near Calcutta, on the banks of the Ganges.

Asutosh Mukerjee Road.description: A street in Calcutta, named after a prominent Bengali academic.

Lucknow.description: A city in northern India; here, refers to the destination of the express train.

China Town.description: China Town (also spelled China-Town or referred to as Chinese City) is a district in Calcutta known for its Chinese community, restaurants, and cuisine.

Bengalis.description: The people of Bengal, or the Bengali language.

rupee.description: The rupee is the currency of India, referenced in both singular and plural forms throughout the novel.

gramophone.description: An early device for playing recorded music, predecessor to the record player.

idolaters.description: A derogatory term used here for Hindus, referring to the worship of idols.

huka.description: A water pipe used for smoking tobacco, also known as hookah.

carri.description: A variant spelling of 'curry,' a dish made with a blend of spices, often including turmeric.

inter-class ticket.description: A railway ticket for a class between third and second class, used in colonial Indian trains.

creolin.description: A disinfectant liquid, here used in a suicide attempt.

Jenia Isaac.description: Jenia Isaac is a Finnish Jewish woman from Capetown, South Africa, who arrives at the narrator's Himalayan bungalow seeking spiritual fulfillment; she is also referred to simply as Jenia.

Himalayas.description: A vast mountain range in Asia, forming the northern border of the Indian subcontinent.

Almora.description: A hill station in the Indian state of Uttarakhand, located in the Himalayas.

Ranikhet.description: A hill station and cantonment town in Uttarakhand, India, near Almora.

Simla.description: Also known as Shimla, a hill station and the capital of Himachal Pradesh, India.

Naini-Tal.description: A popular hill station in Uttarakhand, India, known for its scenic lake.

Fatehpur-Sikhri.description: A historic city near Agra, India, known for its Mughal architecture and now largely abandoned.

Java.description: An island in Indonesia, mentioned as a possible destination for the narrator.

Maikhali.description: A location in the Himalayas, mentioned as a destination for Jenia Isaac.

Bhadrinath.description: A holy town and pilgrimage site in Uttarakhand, India, famous for its Hindu temple.

Hardwar.description: Also known as Haridwar, a sacred city in Uttarakhand, India, and a gateway to the Himalayas.

Kotwara.description: A town or station in northern India, suggested as a travel route.

Capetown.description: A city in South Africa, Jenia Isaac's hometown.

Johannesburg.description: A major city in South Africa, where Jenia performed as a cellist.

Ramacharaka.description: The pseudonym of William Walker Atkinson, an early 20th-century American writer on yoga and occultism, whose books inspired Jenia.

Tibet.description: A region in Asia, often associated with mysticism and spiritual secrets in Western imagination.

Abelard and Heloise.description: Historical figures known for their tragic love affair in medieval France, referenced as a literary parallel.

poste restante.description: A mail service where letters are held at a post office until collected by the recipient.

memsahib.description: A respectful term used in colonial India for a European woman, especially the wife of a sahib.

fakir.description: A term for a Muslim or Hindu ascetic or holy person, often associated with mystical powers.

theosophy.description: A spiritual movement blending Eastern and Western religious ideas, popular in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

bovarism.description: A psychological term derived from Flaubert's 'Madame Bovary,' meaning dissatisfaction with one's life and a tendency to live in fantasies.

Mrs. Mctyre.description: A woman who is annoyed by the narrator's ongoing connection to Maitreyi and expresses her frustration bluntly.

J..description: Mrs. Sen’s nephew, whom the narrator meets in Singapore; he brings news of Maitreyi's fate.

Maika.description: A family member of Maitreyi, possibly her mother, who is described as almost mad with grief over Maitreyi's situation.

Bhowanipore Park.description: A park in the Bhowanipore neighborhood of Calcutta, suggested as a possible meeting place for the narrator and Maitreyi.

Singapore.description: A Southeast Asian city-state, where the narrator hopes to find work and eventually travels.

Burma Oil Company.description: A British colonial-era oil company operating in South and Southeast Asia, where the narrator seeks employment.

Technical Institute Library.description: A library associated with a technical institute, where the narrator researches the job of a river agent.

State Express 555.description: A popular British brand of cigarettes, considered a luxury item in colonial India.

bara-sahibs.description: A term used to refer to high-ranking European men, especially British colonial officials.

idolater.description: A person who worships idols; used here as a derogatory term for someone who has abandoned Christianity.

river agent.description: A job title in colonial India, referring to someone who manages or oversees river transport and trade.
